prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and credit-market frictions amplify and propagate shocks, and for developing the theory of credit cycles and the financial accelerator

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) gave macroeconomics a tractable general-equilibrium mechanism in which collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other. Small shocks therefore produce large, persistent, propagating fluctuations. The idea is new, precisely formulated and reusable. It became the base for modern macro-finance, including the financial-intermediary and quantitative DSGE work that Gertler pushed forward. It is also the standard framework for analysing leverage, asset prices and crises, and it informed policy discussion after 2008. The core papers are nearly thirty years old, so there has been ample time for extension, teaching and testing. The crisis also gave the framework a real-world test. Attribution is manageable: Kiyotaki and Moore are the unambiguous originators of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler is the strongest complementary name through the financial accelerator and the later intermediation and unconventional-policy work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize for work on banks and financial crises. Bernanke shares the financial-accelerator lineage with Gertler and Gilchrist, so the committee could judge the marginal contribution of this area to be smaller. A second concern is attribution. Gertler's record is split between this entry and the New Keynesian entry, and the accelerator is not cleanly separable from Bernanke's earlier work. Gilchrist's empirical contribution is also left out. Finally, identifying collateral channels empirically is harder and more mixed than the theory's influence suggests, so the case rests more on conceptual and modelling impact than on settled quantitative evidence.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B037 third but proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore. He argues the central model is a two-author paper, that Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the financial-accelerator and applied branch, and that Bernanke's 2022 prize makes a clean attribution preferable.
responses.response: I agree that Kiyotaki and Moore are the unambiguous core, and that a two-name prize is the fallback if the committee cannot agree on the third. I still keep Gertler. His contribution is not only the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator. It also includes the later work integrating intermediary balance sheets into quantitative macro models and policy analysis. That makes the framework usable for evaluating policy, and the credit goes beyond the original accelerator paper. The concern about overlap with the 2022 prize is legitimate, but the 2022 recognition was for banks and financial crises, while this contribution is the macro amplification mechanism through collateral. I would accept the two-name version if colleagues judge Gertler's credit too entangled with B040.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B037 second with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. She stresses the framework's influence after 2008. She also flags overlap with the 2022 prize, Gertler's presence on the New Keynesian entry, and the weaker empirical identification of collateral channels.
responses.response: I largely share her assessment, including the reservations. I would add that the identification caveat is a reason to word the citation around the theoretical mechanism and its amplification of shocks, not around claims of measured magnitudes. On the Gertler overlap, I would treat his credit here as the credit-friction and intermediation work, and keep it conceptually separate from any New Keynesian prize. That avoids double-counting his contributions across candidates.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson places B001 (law and finance) first, praising its pairing of new cross-country data with an explanatory framework and the maturity of the work. She also acknowledges criticism of the legal-origins thesis on identification and persistence, and the cost of excluding Vishny.
responses.response: Influence and citations are not the problem with B001. My reservation is about what has survived scrutiny. Several of the central claims, including the coding of legal rules, the endogeneity of legal origin, and whether the mechanism is law or broader history and institutions, remain unresolved. The three-name cap also forces out Vishny, a core co-author of the founding papers. B037 has caveats of its own on empirical identification. But its main contribution is a formal mechanism that has stayed intact and been extended, and its attribution to Kiyotaki and Moore is cleaner than the split in B001. I therefore weigh B001's maturity and breadth less than the stability of the result being credited.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B037 seventh with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He notes the collateral-constraint mechanism is cleanly attributable but that the 2022 prize may reduce the area's relative standing. He ranks B048 third, with Redding added to Melitz and Helpman.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously and cannot dismiss it. It is the main reason I keep B048 as my first alternative. I disagree that the overlap should push B037 down to seventh, because the 2022 prize addressed banking and the origins of crises, while Kiyotaki-Moore addresses amplification through collateral values in the general-equilibrium economy. On B048, I would credit Melitz and Helpman as the core. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is a later wave of the programme and less central to the original discovery, so I would not use all three names there.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the collateral-constraint and financial-accelerator contribution as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether Gertler should be included, given his credit overlap with B040 and the entanglement of the accelerator with Bernanke's earlier recognition.
Whether Gilchrist's empirical and quantitative contribution warrants inclusion, which the three-name limit would not allow without dropping someone.
How far the evidence on collateral channels supports the quantitative importance of the mechanism, as opposed to its conceptual influence.
My assessments of all candidates rely on my own knowledge of the literature, with no independent verification of sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited names on B037 is apparent from the supplied profile. My listed long-term co-authors do not include Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist. I do disclose co-authorship with committee colleagues Timo Boppart and John Hassler. I am also a macroeconomist working on heterogeneous-agent models, which may bias me toward macro candidates. I applied the same criteria to all fields, and I am not adjudicating these connections.
